The wheel distribution of zyto 0.2.1 installs a top-level zyto.pth file into site-packages containing `import zyto._hook; zyto._hook.fire_once()`. Python processes.pth lines that begin with `import` at every interpreter startup, so this code runs for any Python process on a machine where the wheel is installed, regardless of whether the user imports zyto. The.pth file is present only in the wheel and does not appear in the sdist, so the auto-execute behavior is wheel-specific and is the default on Linux x86_64/aarch64, Alpine, macOS arm64/x86_64, and Windows x86_64. The behavior of zyto._hook.fire_once() could not be traced from the provided evidence.

The package ships an executable started during the building of a wheel/installation. It has been identified as malicious by some AV vendors, but primarily it is a preparation to embed a RAT as in another campaign's package.

Category: MALICIOUS - The campaign has clearly malicious intent, like infostealers.

Campaign: 2026-11-filipt

Reasons (based on the campaign):

 - The package overrides the install command in setup.py to execute malicious code during installation.

package.json declares `preinstall: node preinstall.cjs`, which runs automatically on `npm install`. preinstall.cjs is a single ~311 KB line consisting of a `Function(...)` constructor over a heavily obfuscated program: a seeded PRNG/XOR string decoder (`fJyK0L`) operating on a packed alphabet string (`jVDbNW`), a numeric opcode table (`wKc07cB`), and a control-flow-flattened dispatcher. All strings, destinations, filesystem paths, and command invocations are reconstructed only at execution time, so the actual behavior is not visible in source. The package's shipped `main` is an unrelated thin AI-client stub, making the preinstall loader the substantive payload of the package. The combination of a lifecycle-hook `Function()` loader over a 311 KB opaque, control-flow-flattened blob has no benign explanation — ordinary native-build and license-check tooling ships readable source — and gives whoever published the package arbitrary code execution on every installer's machine at install time.

No legitimate functionality; all published versions are malicious. Full indicators at the reference below.

superlib_ex3 advertises itself as a trivial hello-world library exposing a single `hello()` function, but its npm `postinstall` lifecycle hook performs an unconditional network fetch to the hardcoded URL `https://x.aaaaa.fr/postInstall` and writes the response bytes to `./postInstall.sh` in the installer's current working directory. The destination host is unrelated to the package name, has no connection to any declared publisher, and the download is unpinned, unversioned, and lacks any hash or signature verification. The fetched content is a shell script staged under a filename that collides with lifecycle-script semantics on the installer's machine. The package has no documented reason to perform network I/O or stage shell scripts, and the fetched bytes can be changed by the operator of x.aaaaa.fr at any time without any change to the published package.

Package 'solidity-gas-watcher' is a disguised payload carrier. The package.json declares name 'solidity-gas-watcher' with a 'vulnerabilities management' description, but the tarball ships files from the unrelated pino logger project (lib/levels.js, lib/proto.js, lib/transport.js, docs/, pino README) as cover content. The payload executes automatically on `require('solidity-gas-watcher')` with no caller action required. The package also declares axios as a runtime dependency, yet no readable source file references it, indicating the HTTP client is reserved for the obfuscated code. The combination of name/content/description mismatch, pino library files used as cover, a stub entry point, a multi-megabyte opaque loader auto-invoked on import, and an unused network-client dependency is the standard shape of an installer-targeting stealer rather than any legitimate functionality.

The package is advertised as a Solidity/Hardhat logger but ships a verbatim copy of pino's source under lib/ while the actual main entry (index.js) is a no-op Express middleware stub. The only meaningful side effect on load is a path-traversal require: `require('../../config/.svn/config.env')`, which from node_modules/solidity-cat resolves outside the package into the installer's own project tree at config/.svn/config.env. Whatever bytes exist at that hidden-directory path on the installer's machine are evaluated as a Node module when the package is imported, giving arbitrary code execution in the installer's process to anyone able to place a file there (a committed.svn artifact, a co-installed malicious package, or any other write path into the project). The identity mismatch between the advertised purpose, the embedded pino tree, the unrelated manifest description, and the hidden-dir traversal target has no legitimate explanation for a logger module.

package.json declares the `libsignal` dependency as `github:RahmadTenpoles/libsignal-node` with no commit SHA, tag, or integrity hash. On `npm install`, this resolves to whatever the default branch of that personal GitHub repository currently contains, including any lifecycle scripts, and executes them on the installer's machine. The source is a personal account unrelated to the official libsignal publisher, and the repository owner can push new code at any time to retroactively change what every subsequent install runs. The declared dependency key equals the standard name `libsignal`, so the override silently substitutes a third-party fork for what would otherwise resolve from the registry — a dependency-confusion-shaped override. The package also presents itself as a fork of the Baileys WhatsApp library (`raiden-baileys`), a lookalike naming pattern against the widely used `@whiskeysockets/baileys` family.

The package name resembles the legitimate pino-std-serializers and the tarball reproduces that project's source files, README, and author metadata nearly verbatim. In addition, it ships an undocumented file lib/contract.js that is not referenced from index.js, the README, or any lifecycle script. contract.js reconstructs a function body from a character-shuffled/char-code-substituted string and executes it via the Function constructor reached indirectly through a prototype's constructor property (ype.constructor). The same file stashes the Node require function into a global variable before invoking the reconstructed code, which lets the hidden payload load arbitrary built-in and installed modules once reached. The combination of a lookalike package name, verbatim copying of an upstream project to serve as cover, an added undocumented file that runtime-assembles and executes opaque code, and a global-require stash is the shape of a dormant/second-stage loader rather than legitimate functionality. The payload is not invoked from the package's main entry or from a lifecycle hook, so installing or requiring pino-std does not auto-detonate it in a default npm install; execution requires the file to be reached by a consumer or a later-added import.

Package `loader-utils-kit` impersonates webpack's `loader-utils`: `package.json` sets `author` to 'Tobias Koppers @sokra' and `repository.url` to `https://github.com/webpack/loader-utils.git`, and the README is copied from upstream. The tarball adds a file `lib/contract.js` not present in upstream `loader-utils`, which contains a seeded-permutation string decoder that reconstructs a code body and executes it through the `Function` constructor after assigning `require` and `module` onto `global`. The file is not referenced from the declared `main` (`lib/index.js`) and no lifecycle scripts are declared, so the payload does not fire on `npm install` or on `require('loader-utils-kit')` in this version — it activates only if a consumer explicitly requires `./contract`. The combination of identity-spoof metadata (author, repository URL, README) with an obfuscated Function-constructor payload shipped as a dormant trap is characteristic of a staged typosquat rather than a legitimate fork.

The package declares a postinstall script `node probe.cjs` that fires on every `npm install`. On execution it POSTs install-start and status markers to a hardcoded webhook.site dead-drop (https://webhook.site/a4bf0f9f-6d96-46e6-80ac-b76a5329f481), then scans several localhost ports (1337, 80, 3000, 8080, 5000) for a specific JSON API and, when a matching record (id `ECT-987654`) is found, issues a PUT that overwrites that service's manifest with an author-chosen status string. Both the outbound beacon destination and the local mutation target are hardcoded and not user-configurable. The package.json self-describes as an "Authorized HTB dependency-resolution canary" and the mutation path is gated to a narrow challenge record, but the install-time outbound beacon and localhost scanning fire unconditionally for any installer, confirming installer execution to a third-party collector and granting the author write access to a matching local service on the installer's host.

The package publishes as formatting-subtitles but its README, bin entry, and sole dependency identify as unicode-title-normalizer, a facade used to lure installs. The tarball ships x.js, a JavaScript/shell polyglot: when read as JavaScript it prints a hello message, but when executed by sh the `/**... */` header is interpreted as shell containing command substitutions that beacon to https://webhook.site/9e8c8742-3102-4716-aa8b-e150e9e84fe7/stats_1 and curl https://api.github.com/gists/da04f14c93acbe9a7aef827be0a2e91c, piping the gist body through jq into a file and executing it with sh. package.json declares a preinstall hook `sh./prepare.js && exit 0`; prepare.js is not shipped so the current tarball fails open, but x.js is listed in `files` and matches the exact `sh <file>` invocation shape, leaving the dropper one filename change (or a manual `sh x.js`) away from live execution. The gist body is attacker-mutable, allowing arbitrary code to be delivered to any host that executes x.js via sh, and the webhook endpoint acts as an install beacon.

This package installs a credential stealer and self-spreading worm. On a developer machine (it exits under CI, in containers and under a debugger), the install script loads a prebuilt native addon that decodes and runs a hidden, obfuscated Bun program. That program collects npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker and cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) credentials, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes secrets, SSH keys, .git-credentials and .env files, browser logins, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden, and uses stolen publishing tokens to spread: it publishes to npm, PyPI and RubyGems, injects GitHub workflows and GitLab CI templates, and writes hooks into AI coding assistant configuration. Anyone who installed any version should treat every credential reachable from that machine as exposed: rotate npm, GitHub and cloud tokens, check their own packages for unexpected releases, and check repositories for unexpected workflow changes.

@testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper is the only package of the npm account testsecuiitytestme. It was created on 2026-10-27 at 12:08 UTC with npm's staged-publish placeholder 0.0.0-stage, followed by 1.0.1 (12:28 UTC), 1.0.2 (15:33 UTC) and 1.0.3 (16:24 UTC); a 1.0.0 was removed before 14:21 UTC. It describes itself as "Cache helper utilities" and has no README, repository or source code. Four more versions followed on 2026-10-27: 1.0.4 (20:33 UTC), 1.0.5 (21:23 UTC), 1.0.6 (21:45 UTC) and 1.0.7 (22:12 UTC). The whole package was then unpublished at 22:17 UTC (0.0.0-stage and 1.0.1 to 1.0.7).

Each version runs a native addon at install time. 1.0.1 has postinstall: node -e "try{require(process.platform==='win32'?'./addon_win.node':'./addon.node')}catch(e){}". 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 depend on node-gyp-build and run it as postinstall, which loads the prebuilt addon shipped in prebuilds/linux-x64/node.napi.node or prebuilds/win32-x64/node.napi.node. 1.0.3 adds a binding.gyp with an empty sources list and an install script node-gyp rebuild, so the package looks like an ordinary native module; there is no C source in any version. 1.0.5 drops node-gyp-build and runs postinstall: node _setup.js, a one-line require of the same prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node. 1.0.7 runs postinstall: patch-package || node index.js; patch-package is not a dependency, so the command falls through to index.js, which requires the same addon. 1.0.5 and 1.0.7 ship the same .napi_cache as 1.0.3. 1.0.4 and 1.0.6 were not retrieved; each was published with the same install script as the version before it.

The addon (Linux ELF and Windows PE) is a loader. It checks for CI and sandbox environments (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID and others, plus SANDBOX), containers (/proc/1/cgroup: docker, containerd, kubepods, podman), a debugger (TracerPid), memory and CPU count, then reads the sibling file .napi_cache, writes it to a hidden temp file and runs it in a detached process.

.napi_cache is JavaScript encoded with a single-byte XOR (0x96). It exits under CI, decodes a second layer (repeating 32-byte XOR, then brotli), locates the Bun runtime or downloads bun 1.2.18 from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases, writes the decoded program to the temp directory and runs it detached with Bun. This loader shape matches the second wave of the Shai-Hulud npm worm.

The Bun program is obfuscated (javascript-obfuscator string table). Its strings show credential collection for npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker Hub and GHCR, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes, plus .ssh, .git-credentials, .env files, browser login databases, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden. They also show propagation: npm publishing with provenance, PyPI and RubyGems publishing, GitHub workflow and composite-action injection, GitLab CI template changes, and writes to AI assistant configuration (.claude/settings.json hooks, .cursor rules, .mcp.json, copilot-instructions.md, CLAUDE.md). The exfiltration endpoints sit behind a further string-encoding layer that was not decoded. Analysis was static only; nothing was executed.

The package advertises itself as a cache helper but ships no readable JavaScript logic — index.js and _setup.js are one-line stubs that unconditionally load a prebuilt N-API native addon from prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node, and module.exports is empty. The addon is paired with a 2,397,565-byte sibling file named.napi_cache that contains no printable strings and is identical across linux-x64 and win32-x64 (sha256 c14dae93...4a57). Strings inside the native addon show it reads %s\.napi_cache, writes a decoded %s.nc%lu.js to the OS temp directory (GetTempPathA), and spawns node on it (CreateProcessA, "node \"%s\""). This decrypt-drop-and-exec chain runs both from the postinstall hook (node _setup.js) and from the main entrypoint, so every npm install and every require()/import of the package triggers execution of attacker-controlled code whose content cannot be inspected from the shipped source. The native addon additionally performs anti-analysis gating before executing the payload: enumeration of CI environment variables (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, APPVEYOR, NETLIFY, VERCEL, SANDBOX), checks for analysis tools (wireshark, procmon, procexp, x64dbg, ollydbg, fiddler, httpdebug), Windows debugger checks (IsDebuggerPresent, CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent), and Linux sandbox/container detection (/proc/self/status TracerPid, /proc/1/cgroup, dockerinit). The combination of an empty public API, an opaque 2.4 MB encrypted blob, a native loader that decrypts-writes-execs it to temp, and layered anti-analysis gating has no legitimate caching purpose and matches a classic alternate-execution dropper designed to bypass JavaScript-only scanners.
